title: A New Perspective on Classification: Optimally Allocating Limited Resources to Uncertain Tasks
authors: Toon Vanderschueren, Bart Baesens, Tim Verdonck, Wouter Verbeke
conclusions: Formalizes optimal allocation of limited, stochastic resource capacity to tasks with uncertain (binary) outcomes as a linear assignment problem, with capacity modeled as a random variable W converted to a monotonically decreasing sequence of worker success rates.
Proves that, given predicted task rewards, the optimal assignment is simply sorting tasks by predicted reward and assigning greedily in that order (Theorem 4.1).
Proposes an integrated predict-and-optimize approach using learning-to-rank (LambdaMART/NDCG with cost-sensitive relevance) instead of the conventional two-stage classify-then-assign pipeline.

Empirically shows the integrated ranking model (csLambdaMART) achieves higher expected profit, and LambdaMART higher expected precision, than classification baselines (xgboost/csboost) across churn, credit-scoring, marketing, and fraud datasets.

The setting is inductive and probabilistic throughout: capacity is a known/estimated stochastic distribution and the method steers expected profit/cost trade-offs; there is no hard, exactly-enforced count constraint on any fixed test set.
our_use: main.tex:196, in the 'Post-hoc correction and resource allocation' paragraph: '...predict-and-optimize ranking under stochastic capacity \citep{vanderschueren2024perspective}, steering expected costs rather than enforcing a hard count...' -- cited as an example of resource-allocation work that folds a capacity budget into learning (via predict-and-optimize ranking) but only steers expected outcomes probabilistically rather than guaranteeing an exact count, in contrast to TraLO's hard transductive count constraint.
issues: Relevance and the core claim (integrated predict-and-optimize ranking under stochastic, not hard, capacity; no exact count guarantee) are accurate and well-supported by the paper (Sec 2 'Stochastic capacity', Sec 4.2, Theorem 4.1). Minor wording nit: our text says the method 'steer[s] expected costs', but the paper's stated objective throughout is maximizing expected PROFIT (Title, Sec 5); the cost-sensitive relevance label r_i does derive from a cost/profit matrix, so 'costs' is not a hallucination but 'expected profit' would be the more precise term the paper itself uses. Not severe enough to be a mismatch.
